data.title: iMerit’s Radha Basu on how AI is reshaping India’s data annotation jobs
data.description:
Data annotation jobs are becoming increasingly vital in providing jobs to people from tier 2 and 3 cities in India.

Data annotation jobs are where workers repeatedly feed data into AI models and direct them to understand it correctly.

India's data annotation tools market was worth $138 million in 2026 and is expected to reach $648 million in 2031, according to Ken Research.

While data annotation is currently providing job opportunities to a lot of people, there are fears that as models become more sophisticated, it will remove the need for the current workers in the field.

In a conversation with Invezz, Radha Ramaswami Basu, Executive Vice President and Head of iMerit, an EXL Company, discusses how the growing adoption of artificial intelligence is changing the nature of data annotation jobs rather than simply eliminating them.

She explains how workers in India's tier 2 and tier 3 cities can move from routine labelling tasks to specialised roles in model evaluation, red teaming and human oversight, while examining the opportunities and challenges facing India's AI workforce.

Invezz: There are many fears that AI is going to replace jobs, and that includes people who annotate data as models become more sophisticated and perfect. There are also fears that AI increases productivity, and fewer people are required to do a task that needed more people in the past. How would you respond to these claims? Could you provide a counterargument to this claim?

Realistically, no one has been able to state for sure how this will play out.

We can provide some observations from being a part of the industry with a focus on human experts and their role in the AI stack.

First, AI is heavily dependent on human input, human expertise, and human oversight.

We do not expect this to go away. But we expect that this will become more advanced, more nuanced and require both judgment and nuance.

In our own space, routine data labeling, such as drawing boxes around cars, is being automated.

People who previously did that work will need to move to harder tasks where the situations are more complex and multidimensional.

Instead of assessing whether something is a car in an image, the expert has to assess what actions the car may and should take or what to do if there is a sudden emergency.

The work becomes more descriptive and subjective, and checking the work becomes even more advanced. Knowing what “right answer” looks like becomes non-trivial.

As a model becomes more capable, the cost of its mistakes rises, and so does the need to check it.

A model that drafts emails needs light review. A model that approves a loan, reads a scan, or steers a car needs people who can show it was right.

Every model update also has to be evaluated again, because a fix in one area can break another.

Demand is moving toward expertise. A few years ago, most requests we received were for large teams to label images.

Today, clients increasingly ask for physicians to check a model’s clinical reasoning, lawyers to test its reading of a contract, and mathematicians to find the flaw in a proof.

Coders are writing fewer basic functions and instead are reviewing, correcting and approving more complex behaviours generated by AI.

A labor market is forming around expert judgment both in high tech and in the enterprise.

It demands speed, accuracy, and cognitive load, all having value in the market.

People with early experience who grow with it become super-valuable.

On productivity, history suggests that when a task gets cheaper, it gets used more.

Companies apply AI to more problems, more languages, and more countries, and each launch brings new evaluation needs.

The roles are changing faster than they are disappearing. Our job is to make sure people change with them.

Invezz: AI is expected to bring a lot of benefits to robotics. In your view, how quickly can robotics become sophisticated enough to start doing work that is currently dangerous for humans to do

Robots already do some of this work in repetitive, controlled settings, such as pipeline inspection, assembly plants, warehouse logistics, and handling chemical materials.

Now the next frontier is operating in unpredictable environments. A factory floor follows rules. A farm field, a mine, or a construction site changes every hour.

We worked with an agricultural robotics company to take its weeding system from early experiments to an advanced AI product.

Close to a million images were annotated over the engagement, and the system grew to recognize hundreds of plant types, with clear gains in detection accuracy and in how well it handled new conditions.

Better tooling and automation cut completion time for the most complex scenes by 61 percent, and real-time monitoring let the team spot and correct edge cases quickly. 

That last point is the strategic one.

The first 99 percent of training teaches a system what it will usually see.

The last 1 percent is where trust is earned: the weed that looks like a crop seedling, the plant half covered in mud, the field under harsh light.

A robot also has to combine camera, LiDAR, and other sensor data into one consistent picture of the same moment.

Data can look correct on a screen and still fail in the field. Human judgment tells the two apart.

Progress will come workflow by workflow. Narrow, repetitive work in tough conditions will move first, likely within the next few years.

Work that requires a robot to improvise will take longer. Until then, the most reliable setup is a robot doing the physical work with a human ready to step in remotely.

Invezz: India supplies a large share of the world's annotation workforce. As routine labeling gets automated, what happens to entry-level annotators in smaller cities? What does the career path look like from a basic labeling role to an expert evaluator, and how is iMerit helping people make that move?

Smaller cities are where much of India’s new work is happening.

The Quess Pulse Report for the first half of fiscal 2026 found that 69 percent of payroll-linked employment is in Tier 2 and Tier 3 cities.

Tier 3 towns alone account for 40 percent of the workforce and Tier 2 hubs for 29 percent, compared with 31 percent in Tier 1 cities. The future of AI work in India will be decided there.

Routine labeling is being automated, and entry-level roles are changing with it. Inside iMerit, four kinds of roles are growing:

  • Ground truth builders turn images, video, documents, sensor data, and medical scans into data a model can learn from. They also write the prompt and response pairs used to tune a model.
  • Model evaluators assess what a model produces, correct it, and track patterns of failure with every update.
  • Red teamers test a model in creative ways and document exactly where it fails, often across languages and cultures as AI reaches new countries.
  • Human in the loop experts step in once a model is live. When an AI system in insurance, finance, or medicine is uncertain, the decision comes to them.

A new team member now starts by checking and correcting what a model produces.

From there, people specialize in a field such as LiDAR, medical imaging, or a regional language, then move into evaluation, red teaming, and project leadership.

About 3,200 people work with us full-time, and 90 percent of them are in India.

Around that core is a network of more than 30,000 curated experts, our Scholars, who join projects when their expertise is needed.

The full-time team gives us consistency and quality over the long term. The Scholar network gives us reach into almost any field a model needs to learn.

The most important change in India is the kind of work being done.

For a global pharmaceutical company, pathologists in India handled first-pass annotation of tissue slides, and US subspecialists reviewed their work.

Indian talent is moving from processing data to shaping clinical judgment for global medicine. Across every role, expert judgment is what keeps AI safe and reliable.

Invezz: Your Scholars network includes physicians, linguists, scientists, and engineers. As models get better, does the value of human data go up or down, and why?

It goes up. Better models make more convincing mistakes.

A fluent answer to a medical or financial question can still be wrong, and catching it takes a physician or a mathematician with years of practice.

AI development is also shifting.

The focus is moving from building ever more capable foundation models to adapting them for specific uses, especially in regulated industries like healthcare, banking, and insurance.

That work depends on experts who can challenge a model before it reaches customers.

We call it tormenting models. We question the model, question it again to make sure it is working, and actually try to break it.

That is why we built the iMerit Scholars platform on Ango Hub.

Our community includes more than 30,000 vetted experts across 118 countries and 106 languages, and the platform is designed to grow to hundreds of thousands.

Every Scholar goes through a three-tier assessment. The first screens general AI capability and cognitive skills.

The second tests domain qualifications and the ability to work effectively with AI models. The most specialized roles add peer review by other experts in the field.

Being part of EXL gives us access to deeper healthcare and insurance expertise, which strengthens our ability to support AI built for specific enterprises.

Our biggest need right now is to go into new expertise, scale into newer languages, and into newer levels of the same expertise.

The next phase of generative AI will be won by those who treat expertise as human capital. Technology should make that expertise easier to reach, retain, and apply.

Invezz: In areas like healthcare AI and autonomous vehicles, a flawed training set can cause real harm. What does iMerit do to catch bias, errors, and blind spots in data before they reach a model?

Most harmful errors in training data are systematic.

A category is defined poorly, a condition is missing, or reviewers read the same thing in different ways. We focus on catching these patterns early, and the work starts with who checks the data and how.

In healthcare, the standard is clinical truth. Our open-source 3D mammography dataset, released in 2026, covers 558 patients, 271 with malignant findings and 287 with benign ones.

Every case is confirmed by biopsy and reviewed by US board-certified radiologists.

The average tumor is 1.34 cm, and 85 percent of lesions are under 2 cm.

This helps a model learn from early cancers, which are the hardest to detect. On every scan, a radiologist has marked the exact boundary between a lesion and healthy tissue.

That judgment is now part of the data. Fast Company recognized the dataset in its Next Big Things in Tech 2026 list. 

In autonomous mobility, the standard is consistency across people, sensors and regions.

On one program covering images, video and 3D LiDAR across the US, Europe and Asia Pacific, LiDAR accuracy was stuck near 80 percent.

Our specialists held weekly calibration sessions so reviewers made the same calls, and added a two-stage quality check.

They also revised the taxonomy, adding classes for road objects the model kept missing and removing ones that added noise. Accuracy rose above the client’s 95 percent threshold.

That’s the main reason clients choose to work with iMerit. In high-stakes situations, you want professionalism, accountability, and consistency.

Invezz: Will AI mostly benefit large labs and wealthy countries, or can it spread opportunity more widely? How can countries like India participate in AI as creators and shapers of models, and not just as a source of low-cost labor?

The foundations of AI, such as compute and capital, are concentrated today. The value of AI, however, depends on how well it understands the people it serves.

That understanding comes from everywhere.

A model becomes truly useful when it understands a patient’s history, a farmer’s soil, or a customer’s language.

That knowledge lives with doctors, agronomists, linguists and engineers around the world. 

India also has a long tradition of knowing how to do global business - listening to the customer; understanding the problem; solving the problem.

This is very important in applying high-stakes AI in the enterprise.

India brings a deep pool of scientific and professional talent, 22 scheduled languages and a large population whose needs AI must learn to serve.

The greatest opportunity lies in defining how models are evaluated, building datasets that reflect Indian realities, and developing domain models for healthcare, agriculture, and finance.

Those who set the standards will shape what AI becomes.

I have always believed that true breakthroughs happen at the intersection of people and machines. Countries that invest in both will help shape the future of AI.

Invezz: In 2026, iMerit was acquired by EXL. How does pairing your expert data network and Ango Hub platform with EXL's broader data and AI services change what you can offer clients? Where do you see the company’s future moving forward?

I see three directions ahead.

First, it brings frontier lab discipline to regulated industries.

EXL’s clients in insurance, banking, and healthcare will need to show regulators how their models were tested, who reviewed them, and how failures were handled.

iMerit has built that rigor through evaluation, red teaming, and RLHF with foundation model companies. Together, we can help enterprises become audit-ready before the rules arrive.

Second, it connects expert judgment to real workflows.

Ango Hub brings data, experts, and quality checks into one place.

EXL knows how claims, underwriting, and operations run every day. Together, we can tune models to a client’s own processes and data, and keep evaluating them once they are live.

That shortens the path from pilot to production.

Third, it widens where we can grow. iMerit’s work in robotics, autonomous mobility, healthcare AI, and physical AI gives EXL a direct role with foundation model and autonomy companies.

EXL’s scale of nearly 68,000 people gives us the depth to take on larger, longer programs.

Both companies were built the same way, with people at the center and domain expertise as the foundation of good AI.

That common ground is why the integration has felt natural from the start.

data.title: Large-scale employee buyouts are not new, but big tech is changing its meaning
data.description:
In the early 2000s, mobile phones arrived. Soon, communicating through those clunky, stationary telephones was going out of fashion.

The future was here, and Verizon was not ready.

Customers were abandoning landlines for mobile phones in growing numbers.

The company’s traditional business, once a reliable engine of revenue, was steadily eroding.

Hit by regulatory setbacks amid already difficult conditions, Verizon turned to a familiar corporate instrument: the voluntary buyout.

It offered packages to roughly 152,000 employees.

A few years later, Ford did something similar, extending buyout offers to about 75,000 workers while deep in losses and fighting for survival.

These were two companies in structural trouble, trying to shrink their way toward stability.

For decades, large-scale voluntary separation programs carried a clear meaning. Companies were in distress and needed to cut costs.

That meaning is now changing.

Microsoft's hard decision

In late October 2026, Microsoft sent a different kind of message to a large share of its workforce.

Roughly 60,000 employees, about 27% of the company, received a voluntary exit offer.

It was the largest such program in Microsoft's history.

Sixty thousand is a staggering number. But an even more astonishing figure is $36.6 billion.

That was the company's net income in the three months ended September.

Microsoft reported its results just days after making the buyout offers public. The business was roaring.

Revenue reached $92.3 billion, up 19%. Operating income rose to $45.9 billion.

Net income climbed 32% to $36.6 billion. Azure grew 48%. Wall Street estimates were left behind.

On the same day, Alphabet posted its own strong quarter: revenue of $127.6 billion, up 25%, with Google Cloud more than doubling to $30.7 billion.

The company said it was now running at a half-trillion-dollar annual pace.

And yet, this week, Alphabet also confirmed that it was extending its existing buyout program to five more countries.

The financial profiles of both companies remain robust. And yet, they are increasingly turning to the same tool once reserved for periods of decline.

Meta has also used comparable packages in certain markets.

The approach of large-scale buyouts might not be new, but things are definitely changing.

A different way out

People who study how companies manage their workforces say the shift is revealing.

Wayne Cascio, who has researched downsizing for decades, says such exercises have been around since the 1970s. However, he, too, is seeing a shift.

"Voluntary buyouts started in the 1970s, primarily in manufacturing. During the global financial crisis in 2008, they were widely used by all kinds of companies," Cascio said in a recent Harvard Business Review interview.

"What's changing now is the types of people who are being offered buyouts. In the past, companies usually required employees to have reached a minimum age and minimum tenure — say, people over 55 with at least 10 years at the company.

"Effectively, that means most people were usually within a couple of years of qualifying for retirement. We called them buyouts, but they functioned as early retirement programs. Often, they included early vesting or other retirement sweeteners.

"Microsoft's buyouts have no age limitation and almost no tenure requirement. They're being offered to everyone in certain departments. That approach is becoming more common. Having so many people of all ages affected that's different from what we've seen before."

Why are companies choosing buyouts over outright layoffs?

Cascio explains that voluntary buyouts can give employees a greater sense of agency than abrupt job cuts. That sense of control can also help protect the morale of those who remain.

Josh Bersin, a longtime observer of human resources trends, has described Microsoft's program as something closer to a new management model than a traditional layoff.

"What Microsoft has done is not a layoff, rather a thoughtful workforce innovation, one which many companies will want to copy."

The AI connection

Both Microsoft and Alphabet, like almost all major technology companies, are spending enormous amounts to expand their AI ambitions.

To put money into AI, these companies are having to cut costs somewhere. Reducing employee headcount is one of the ways these giant corporations are doing so.

Bersin argues that this is not necessarily a sign of financial weakness.

"This is not the behavior of a company in distress: it's the behavior of a company thinking ahead."

"By creating space for self-selection out of the organization, they [Microsoft] make room to redeploy talent into AI-critical roles, continuing to hire selectively in high-growth areas, and maintain the engagement of those who stay."

In an era of heavy AI investment, corporate leaders face growing pressure to improve productivity metrics, including revenue per employee.

A measured reduction in headcount, achieved through voluntary means, can support those numbers while companies continue to fund their infrastructure buildout.

Bersin sees the approach as a logical response to the dual demands of technological ambition and financial discipline.

What comes next?

The deeper question is: Where are we headed?

Is this a temporary adjustment, a way for companies to finance enormous AI investments without destroying profitability?

Or is it the early version of a more permanent model, in which large technology firms continuously reshape their workforces through voluntary programs rather than following the old cycle of aggressive hiring followed by abrupt job cuts?

Kristalina Georgieva, managing director of the International Monetary Fund, has warned that AI is "like a tsunami hitting the labor market."

IMF research has found that AI is likely to affect around 60% of jobs in advanced economies and 40% globally.

Dario Amodei, CEO of the IPO-bound Anthropic, has predicted that AI could eliminate half of all white-collar jobs and push unemployment to 20%.

A recent study from Stanford Digital Economy Lab, however, found that AI is not yet causing widespread, economy-wide job displacement, but is aggressively squeezing young workers.

There is a firm belief among many that human judgment will continue to be key.

"The idea that companies will no longer need people is an oversimplification. Human judgment, creativity, customer understanding and accountability remain essential," Bajrang Saharan, CEO of Pressmate OS, told Indian publication India Today.

Even amid gloomy forecasts, the World Economic Forum projects that 170 million new roles will emerge over the same period, resulting in a net gain of 78 million jobs worldwide.

However, WEF also cautions that entry-level jobs remain under immense pressure. It believes that "globally, more than one in three young workers are employed in occupations with medium to high exposure to AI-driven task change."

But one thing is for sure. Change is the only constant, and in the age of AI, that change is happening as rapidly as ever.

What has already changed is the signal these programs send. For much of the past half-century, a large voluntary buyout usually meant a company was in trouble.

How far that redefinition reaches will help determine the texture of work in the technology industry for years to come.

The post Large-scale employee buyouts are not new, but big tech is changing its meaning appeared first on Invezz

data.title: Airbnb stock analysis after boosting its revenue and profit guidance
data.description:
Airbnb stock jumped to its highest point since November 2021 after the company published strong financial results. It jumped to $193, up by 136% from its lowest point on record, with its valuation rising to over $110 billion. This rally may continue in the near future. 

Airbnb published strong financial results

ABNB stock continued its strong rally after releasing its third-quarter earnings report. This report showed that its revenue jumped by 19% to $4.9 billion, with its net income soaring by 38% to $1.9 billion. These numbers were better than what most analysts were expecting. 

Most notably, the company said that its free cash flow (FCF) rising by nearly 30% to $1.4 billion, with the gross booking value hitting $27.7 billion. These numbers showed that its revenue growth gained momentum, which is rare for a company of its size. 

The company also hinted that the growth will continue in the coming quarters, helped by its innovation. It now expects that its fourth-quarter revenue will jump to between $3.22 billion and $3.28 billion, up by between 16% and 18%. These metrics were better than the average estimate of $3.16 billion.

For the year, the company is expected to grow in the high teens, higher than what analysts were expecting. Analysts were expecting its annual revenue to come in at $14.18 billion. These are encouraging numbers for a company that has not made any acquisitions. 

Instead, the management has continued to innovate, including by allowing hotels to add their rooms to the platform. Thousands of boutique and independent hotels have already signed up so far. It has also added car rentals, which have become popular among users, and partnered with American Express. It also partnered with Meta Platform to use Muse agent.

Analysts have reacted positively to the earnings. Ygal Arounian, a Wedbush analyst, hiked his target from $200 to $237, suggesting a 40% upside. Shyam Patil of Susquehanna hiked the forecast from $200 to $220, while Rosenblatt increased it from $220 to $230. Other analysts who have upgraded the stock recently are from companies like Cantor Fitzgerald, Raymond James, and UBS Group.

Some of these analysts note that the strong growth will help to justify its relatively high valuation. Kyro datashows that the company has a forward price-to-earnings ratio of 32, which is higher than the sector median of 16.

Airbnb stock technical analysis

ABNB stock chart | Source: TradingView

The daily chart shows that the ABNB stock bottomed at $149.5 in September and then started an uptrend. It formed an up-gap today after publishing its financial results.

The stock has moved above the 50-day and 100-day Exponential Moving Averages (EMA). It has also moved above the Supertrend indicator and the median line of the Andrews pitchfork tool.

The stock will likely continue rising in the coming days as investors target the key resistance level of $200. This view will be confirmed if it jumps above the intraday high of $193.

data.title: Nasdaq rebounds 1% as chip stocks recover; Dow falls despite strong jobs data
data.description:
US stocks opened higher on Friday as chipmakers and technology stocks recovered from Thursday’s sharp selloff.

The Nasdaq Composite led the rebound, while Dow Jones remained under pressure, as investors assessed stronger-than-expected jobs data and concerns about potential restrictions on AI infrastructure development.

The recovery followed a bruising session on Wall Street, where the Nasdaq Composite entered correction territory after its steepest one-day decline in 19 months.

Investors were also weighing the implications of the October employment report and the outlook for interest rates.

Chip stocks lead recovery after Thursday's rout

The Nasdaq Composite opened 1% higher while the S&P 500 gained 0.35%. The Dow Jones Industrial Average, however, fell 476 points.

Nvidia rose 5.64% in trading after losing 9% on Thursday, its worst session since January 2025.

Micron Technology gained 5.3% after falling 17% in the previous session.

AMD, Intel and Broadcom also advanced between 5% and 9%.

Data-centre operators IREN and Applied Digital, cloud computing companies CoreWeave and Nebius Group, and energy and equipment suppliers GE Vernova and Constellation Energy also recovered from steep losses.

Tesla and SpaceX shares rose 1.5% and 5%, respectively, after declining sharply over the previous two sessions.

Software company Atlassian moved in the opposite direction, falling 11.5% after reporting its first-quarter results.

Airbnb gained 10.39% after raising its full-year 2026 revenue growth forecast.

The rebound followed Thursday’s broad market decline.

The Nasdaq fell 5.5%, moving more than 10% below its recent high and entering correction territory. The S&P 500 lost 4.4%, while the Dow dropped more than 1,800 points, or 3.4%.

All 11 S&P 500 sectors ended lower.

The Magnificent Seven companies collectively lost $1 trillion in market capitalisation during the session.

AI regulation concerns weigh on market sentiment

The selloff was driven partly by concerns that Democratic gains in the midterm elections could lead to tighter restrictions on data-centre development.

Democratic victories in several key states and control of Congress raised questions about the pace of the AI infrastructure buildout.

Texas, a major data-centre hub, became a particular focus after Governor-Elect Gina Hinojosa indicated that the state would seek stronger protections before allowing further development.

The concerns weighed heavily on semiconductor companies and other businesses exposed to AI infrastructure.

The Nasdaq was also heading for its fourth consecutive weekly decline, while the S&P 500 was on track for its worst weekly performance since March 2025.

The CBOE Volatility Index, Wall Street’s fear gauge, recorded its largest one-day jump in about 19 months on Thursday. It eased slightly on Friday to 26.81.

Strong jobs report puts interest rate outlook in focus

Investors also assessed October employment data, which showed that US nonfarm payrolls increased by 165,000, well above economists’ expectations of 59,000.

The unemployment rate declined to 4.1%, compared with forecasts for it to remain at 4.2%.

The stronger labour market data pushed Treasury yields higher and limited gains in equity markets.

Investors are also monitoring the Federal Reserve’s next policy decision, with traders pricing in a more than 76% chance of an interest rate hike in December, according to the CME FedWatch Tool.

Oil prices added another source of uncertainty after rising on Thursday, raising concerns about energy-driven inflation and the possibility of higher interest rates.

Brent crude futures were broadly flat on Friday, although oil remained on course for a sharp weekly decline.

Despite Friday’s recovery, the Nasdaq and S&P 500 remained down around 4.4% and nearly 3%, respectively, for the week through Thursday.

The Dow was relatively more resilient, with a weekly decline of about 0.5%.

AI disclosure: AI tools assisted with research and drafting of this piece. An Invezz editor reviewed the facts, sources and wording before publication. Any opinions or analysis are Invezz’s, not those of an automated system.

data.title: UPay and WIDTH partner to improve digital asset risk screening
data.description:
As digital asset payment service providers continue to improve financial compliance on their platforms in a fight against money laundering and fraud, there are still gaps left in the ecosystem to address. 

KYC has its limits

KYCs can help ensure platform users are verified, which helps weed out bad actors.

However, knowing your platform users well does not help in building trust in the origin of a transaction depositing funds into a verified user’s wallet.

This can limit the ability to address cross-platform risks.

Financial technology company UPay has announced a partnership with WIDTH, an AI-based compliance and risk decision intelligence platform helping institutions manage financial crime risk.

The partnership will allow UPay to use WIDTH’s on-chain risk screening product, DART, to analyse wallet addresses and transactions, forming the basis for further investigations under UPay’s risk policies.

UPay offers an integrated ecosystem of digital asset services, including digital wallets, payment cards, OTC services, and cross-border settlement and remittance for individuals and businesses. 

Understanding transaction history to identify risk factors

Its partnership with the compliance and risk platform WIDTH aims to help reviewers understand the transaction history and risk connections behind flagged wallet addresses and transactions.

“Our aim is to give reviewers more than a risk flag,” said Owen Yang, CEO of UPay.

“We want them to understand what triggered it and see the transaction history behind it, so they can decide what needs further investigation.”

DART’s wallet address risk screening (KYA) and transaction risk screening (KYT) can be used to assess an address’s risk characteristics and links to high-risk entities, which helps in investigating the sources and destinations of transaction funds.

By using DART,  each result can be traced to its score, matched rules, and transaction paths.

Reviewers then use that information to understand risk flags when conducting a manual review and further investigations under UPay’s own risk policies.

“Our focus is on making risk findings useful to the people reviewing them,” said Chionh Chye Kit, Co-Founder & CEO of WIDTH.

“Scores, matched rules and transaction paths help explain why an address or transaction needs attention.”

UPay and WIDTH said they plan to define DART’s scope for various products and service regions for different applications and use cases, across supported assets, blockchain networks, and business arrangements. Evaluation will be based on feedback from actual use.

According to UPay, DART’s analysis will be used to supplement its own risk review process, rather than replace it.

UPay’s own customer due diligence, independent review, business decisions, or applicable regulatory obligations remain the core of the process.

data.title: Google as we know it is changing
data.description:
When Alphabet GOOGL released its Q3 earnings last month, two figures stood out.

Search advertising, the tech behemoth's largest revenue source, grew by 12%.

That was down from 17% in the second quarter and below the approximately 14% growth analysts had pencilled in.

The figure suggested that the business Google is synonymous with might be losing momentum.

For the first time, Google Search also accounted for less than half of Alphabet's total revenue.

The other side of the results told a very different story.

Google Cloud sales more than doubled to $31 billion, lifting the segment's contribution to the company's top line to 24%, up from 15% a year earlier.

Demand for its tensor processing units (TPUs), Alphabet's answer to Nvidia's GPUs, was reported as strong.

The company also said its Gemini 4 Argon and Carbon models were leading at the frontier.

"Overall, our first-party model APIs are now processing nearly 32 billion tokens per minute, more than four times what we processed a year ago," it said.

The Gemini app also reached one billion users, making it the fastest-growing product in Google's history.

Alphabet said foreign exchange was the biggest factor behind the slowdown in Search growth compared with the second quarter.

However, company executives conceded that AI-powered Search had also played a significant role.

"The strong growth in AI Overviews had an impact because of the lower monetization we were seeing in AI Mode," said Philipp Schindler, Alphabet's chief business officer.

The company acknowledged that queries conducted through AI Mode were, on average, three times longer than traditional searches, but generated lower monetisation for the time being.

While the contrasting numbers for Search and Cloud may have left investors confused, another metric helped complete the picture.

Alphabet reported negative free cash flow of $9.07 billion, substantially worse than the $2.70 billion analysts had expected.

The company also maintained its FY 2026 capital expenditure guidance of $195 billion to $205 billion and expects spending to increase substantially in FY 2027, although management has not provided a numerical range.

Alphabet's stock tanked roughly 13% in its worst single-day drop in company history, wiping out approximately $475 billion to $511 billion in market capitalisation.

For investors, the narrative was set: Alphabet was burning cash to support a technology that was generating rich returns but was also beginning to cannibalise its core Search business, its main cash cow.

“This is the first quarter that the negative thesis around AI crushing search has legs,” Dan Ives, a famously bullish analyst at Yorkville Ives, wrote in an Oct. 30 note.

The company plans to scale advertising within its AI Overviews and AI Mode products going forward.

But the question remains: will Alphabet gradually become known less for Google Search and more as a cloud infrastructure company?

How GenAI turned around Google Cloud's fortunes

When Sundar Pichai replaced Google co-founder Larry Page as CEO in 2019, he identified Google Cloud and YouTube as two major bets that could take Alphabet beyond its dependence on Search advertising.

Since then, YouTube has largely delivered, becoming the world's largest video platform.

Google Cloud, by contrast, struggled for years, losing billions between 2018 and 2022 as Alphabet invested heavily in servers, data centres and chips.

The business finally turned its first profit in 2023.

Generative AI now offers Alphabet an opportunity to accelerate that progress and close the gap with cloud rivals Microsoft and Amazon.

Amazon remains the global market leader, with an approximately 31% share, while Microsoft's Azure holds about 20%.

"This quarter makes a real case that Alphabet can start taking the AI lead from Microsoft (when it comes to cloud)," David Wagner, head of equities at Aptus Capital Advisors, told Invezz.

"Query growth was the strongest in five years, so people are using Search more than ever. Alphabet just isn’t getting paid as much for each query yet, which is exactly the cannibalization investors fear. Ads are now scaling across AI Overviews and AI Mode, including internationally for the first time, and that rollout is the thing to watch," he said.

Google Cloud to soon rival combined strength of Search and YouTube

Wagner, however, conceded that it would not be unreasonable to expect Google Cloud to become Alphabet's primary driver of incremental earnings growth, even as Search remains its largest revenue contributor.

"It’s already happening: Cloud is doing most of the heavy lifting on growth now, and it’s adding more new profit than the entire Search and YouTube side combined, but this was inevitable. Search is still the big cash cow, but Cloud is where the incremental earnings story lives," he said.

He is not alone.

Rosenblatt expects Google Cloud revenue to surpass the combined revenue of Search and YouTube by 2028.

The brokerage believes Alphabet's value is gradually shifting from advertising towards cloud computing, although investors will need time to assess near-term trends and the durability of its Search business.

JPMorgan's Doug Anmuth, meanwhile, believes Google Cloud will become an even more critical part of the business, driving overall Alphabet revenue growth of approximately 30% in both 2027 and 2028.

"AI’s main beneficiary, without a doubt, is Alphabet’s cloud business," said Malik Ahmed Khan of Morningstar, adding that not only is the segment's growth stellar, but its backlog, or future contracted revenue, is also five times its annualised quarterly sales.

This provides the business with significant visibility as it invests in AI infrastructure.

"Within cloud, we see TPUs, Alphabet’s AI accelerators, as a key differentiator. As Alphabet moves from renting out TPUs to actually selling them to external customers, including Anthropic, and recently Oracle, we expect Google Cloud revenue to meaningfully inflect upward," he said.

Should Alphabet split its Cloud and Search businesses?

As investors' reaction to Alphabet's earnings overshadowed the strong Cloud growth, Gil Luria of DA Davidson suggested that the company should split up its Cloud and Search businesses.

"As the stock now trades at 18-19x earnings, you have to ask yourself why do you want to penalise this very fast growing AI business because it's attached to a search business that is now going to be in perpetual slowdown," Luria told CNBC.

Wagner disagrees with the suggestion.

"I don’t buy it, because the whole point is that these businesses feed each other: the same chips, models and research power both Search and Cloud, and Search’s cash flow is what pays for the massive AI build-out. Splitting them would be like separating the engine from the gas tank," he said.

Alphabet must prove AI can monetise Search as Cloud takes centre stage

That interdependence could become increasingly important as Alphabet expands its AI infrastructure.

Cloud and AI solutions may account for a growing share of incremental revenue and earnings, but Search's cash generation will remain crucial to financing that expansion.

Khan said he believed investors were underappreciating the breadth and depth of Alphabet’s AI monetization and the rapid upcoming growth in Google Cloud.

He added that Alphabet’s vertical integration allows it to absorb AI costs better than peers.

"Its in-house TPUs, AI models, and co-design of hardware and software enable it to lower its total cost of ownership. As such, we view the cost-led bear argument against Alphabet to be manageable," he said.

The company's stock remains in the red, down about 9% this year.

Over the past week, analysts have lowered their estimates for Alphabet’s 2026 earnings per share by 4.5%, even if it has made the stock cheaper too.

"Cloud is carrying the story, but until Search shows AI is additive, the stock may be in the penalty box," Wagner said.

The immediate challenge for Alphabet therefore is to prove that AI-powered Search can generate enough advertising revenue to offset changes in how users discover information and shop online.

According to Futurum Research, Alphabet's AI strategy is creating distinct monetisation opportunities across enterprise applications, infrastructure and consumer Search, but each business faces a different execution challenge.

Gemini Enterprise adoption and external TPU distribution could broaden revenue sources beyond traditional cloud consumption, although the profitability of externally deployed hardware remains less transparent.

Meanwhile, longer conversational queries and growing AI Mode engagement have yet to demonstrate advertising economics comparable to traditional Search.

Improving monetisation will therefore be essential to protecting the profitability of Google's core business.

"If enterprise AI spending and TPU deployments generate sufficient returns to absorb rising infrastructure costs while AI Search improves advertising yields, Alphabet could sustain a broader AI growth profile without sacrificing the margins that underpin its investment capacity," it said.

Alphabet's business identity is changing

For now, the outlook for Search continues to divide analysts.

The bears, according to Morningstar, believe the deceleration will remain gradual, giving Alphabet time to adapt its business and "drive the majority of sales from nonsearch businesses within five years".

The bulls and bears may disagree on how quickly Search will lose ground, but they appear to converge on one point: Alphabet's business identity is changing.

"Cloud’s still about half the size of Search, but at the pace it’s growing and with the backlog it’s sitting on, I think they’re neck and neck within a couple of years. So yes, the value is moving, and Alphabet is slowly turning from an ad company with a cloud business into an AI infrastructure company that happens to own the best ad business in the world," Wagner said.

data.title: Star analyst says recent tech rout a 'golden buying opportunity'
data.description:
Tech stocks suffered a sharp sell-off in the wake of the US midterm elections, wiping hundreds of billions of dollars from market values and pushing the Nasdaq Composite into correction territory.

Yet one of Wall Street’s most prominent technology bulls believes investors may be looking at the market all wrong.

According to veteran analyst Dan Ives, the recent decline reflects fear of an AI spending slowdown rather than a genuine threat to the long-term artificial intelligence investment cycle, creating what he called a rare buying opportunity for patient investors.

Why Wall Street suddenly turned soar on AI stocks

The market’s reaction was fueled by concerns that a Democratic sweep of Congress could lead to stricter oversight of large tech companies and increased resistance to the rapid expansion of data centers across the US.

Investors quickly extrapolated that political headwinds could slow construction projects, limit energy approvals, and ultimately reduce demand for the semiconductor and infrastructure firms powering the AI boom.

That fear was particularly visible in high-growth areas of the market.

Chipmakers, cloud software providers, AI infrastructure firms, and data-center operators saw aggressive selling as investors rushed to reassess future earnings expectations.

The concern is understandable: much of the sector’s extraordinary rally over the past two years has been built on assumptions of uninterrupted AI investment.

However, market history shows investors frequently overreact when uncertainty collides with popular themes.

In many cases, short-term political developments create volatility, while long-term technology adoption trends continue largely unaffected.

Dan Ives believes AI spending is not going away

Ives argues the market is treating the election outcome as though it will bring the AI revolution to a halt. In his view, that assumption is disconnected from economic reality.

The analyst wrote that the sell-off appears to be pricing in a scenario where AI infrastructure expansion is effectively stopped, an outcome he considers highly unlikely.

Instead, Ives sees a moderation in the pace of growth rather than a reversal.

His thesis is straightforward: companies that have already committed massive capital to AI cannot afford to step back now.

The race for computing power, AI models, enterprise software integration, and cloud infrastructure remains intensely competitive, and any company that slows spending risks losing strategic ground to rivals.

Importantly, many of the data-center projects driving the AI ecosystem already possess permits, financing, and construction momentum.

Those projects represent billions of dollars of committed investment that would be difficult and costly to unwind.

Ives estimates AI-related capital spending could still reach between $3 trillion and $4 trillion in the coming years, with major technology companies expected to invest heavily even if the political environment becomes less favorable.

The bigger lesson for long-term investors

Perhaps the most intriguing aspect of Ives’ argument is his comparison to previous market panics.

He likened the current sell-off to moments when investor fear overwhelmed fundamentals, including the COVID-driven market collapse in 2020 and the sharp AI-related correction that followed the tariff-driven market shock of April 2025.

In both cases, investors who focused on long-term trends rather than short-term headlines were ultimately rewarded.

The broader investment takeaway is that AI remains one of the most significant capital investment cycles in modern technology history.

While regulatory scrutiny, political opposition, and infrastructure bottlenecks may affect the timing of projects, they are unlikely to eliminate the underlying demand for computing capacity.

Businesses across industries continue increasing their reliance on AI tools, creating a powerful incentive for technology companies to keep building.

For investors, that distinction matters. A slowdown in growth can pressure stock prices for a period, but it is very different from the collapse of an investment theme.

If Ives' outlook proves correct, the recent correction may eventually be remembered not as the start of the AI boom’s end, but as another opportunity for investors to accumulate leading technology names while sentiment remains fragile.

data.title: Evening digest: Gold slips, Anthropic IPO faces valuation cut
data.description:
Global financial markets remained volatile on Friday as stronger-than-expected US employment data lifted the dollar and Treasury yields, putting pressure on gold prices.

Oil was also heading for its steepest weekly decline in years as investors assessed the possibility of de-escalation in the US-Iran conflict.

Meanwhile, Anthropic's proposed blockbuster IPO faced growing uncertainty, with prospective investors reportedly pushing for a lower valuation following the sharp sell-off in AI-related stocks.

US nonfarm payrolls beat estimates, unemployment falls

The US labour market delivered a stronger-than-expected performance in October, adding 165,000 jobs compared with economists' expectations of 59,000.

The unemployment rate declined to 4.1%, while revisions showed that August and September employment growth had been stronger than previously estimated.

Average hourly earnings increased 0.4% month-on-month and 3.1% year-on-year, exceeding expectations and potentially adding to inflation concerns.

The figures strengthened the case for further monetary tightening, with traders raising expectations of a December rate increase.

The report could complicate the Federal Reserve's efforts to balance inflation control with labour market conditions, particularly as stronger wage growth and resilient employment suggest that the economy continues to withstand higher borrowing costs.

Gold prices slip as US payrolls strengthen

Gold prices declined on Friday after stronger-than-expected US nonfarm payrolls data reinforced expectations that the Federal Reserve could keep interest rates higher for longer.

Spot gold fell 0.65% to $4,060.73 an ounce, after dropping more than 1% earlier in the session to a low of $4,033.29.

US gold futures for December delivery settled 0.96% lower at $4,073.90.

Despite Friday's decline, spot gold was up 5.2% for the week, putting it on track for its strongest weekly performance since August.

The US added 165,000 jobs in October, significantly exceeding economists' expectations of 59,000. The unemployment rate also declined to 4.1%, indicating continued resilience in the labour market.

The data strengthened expectations of another Fed rate increase in December. Markets priced in an 81% probability of a hike, compared with 72.8% before the employment report.

A stronger dollar, which climbed to its highest level since October 29, and rising Treasury yields also weighed on bullion.

Higher interest rates increase the opportunity cost of holding non-yielding assets such as gold.

Oil prices post biggest weekly decline since pandemic

Oil prices were heading for a sharp weekly decline as expectations of a potential de-escalation in the US-Iran conflict reduced the geopolitical risk premium in crude markets.

Brent crude futures for January delivery was up 0.20% to $98.51 a barrel on Friday, while US West Texas Intermediate gained 0.54% to $91.04.

Brent was on track to lose approximately 16% for the week, which would mark its steepest weekly percentage decline since the beginning of the Covid-19 pandemic. WTI was heading for a 12% weekly decline.

The Democratic Party's gains in the US midterm elections raised hopes of a potential easing of tensions involving Iran and an increase in crude exports from the region.

However, attacks on vessels in the Gulf and the Strait of Hormuz continued to support prices.

A Greek ship manager reported that a seafarer was killed in an explosion aboard an oil products tanker on November 5, believed to have been caused by a missile attack.

Signs of an emerging supply surplus also weighed on the market, with demand destruction and changing crude supply patterns adding to concerns about oversupply.

Anthropic IPO valuation faces potential $1 trillion reset

Anthropic's proposed initial public offering is facing growing investor resistance as the recent technology stock selloff raises doubts about its expected $1.5 trillion valuation.

At least three major investors believe the AI company may have to lower its valuation, with one suggesting it could be closer to $1 trillion, according to The Wall Street Journal.

The company could also reduce its fundraising target from approximately $100 billion to $80 billion.

The concerns follow a sharp selloff in AI-related stocks, with the Nasdaq Composite falling as much as 5% on Thursday.

Investors are also assessing Anthropic's financial performance and infrastructure commitments.

Its revenue run rate exceeded $80 billion at the end of October, according to the Journal, while its amended IPO filing showed third-quarter revenue of $17 billion.

The company has approximately $895.4 billion in commitments for computing capacity, chips and other infrastructure.

The IPO roadshow was initially expected to begin during the week of November 9, with pricing anticipated the following week.

However, deteriorating market conditions could force the company to reconsider its timetable.

data.title: Why is Moderna stock rising nearly 9% today?
data.description:
Moderna stock MRNA surged nearly 9% on Friday after the company reported a return to profitability in the third quarter and raised its full-year revenue outlook.

The biotechnology company reported revenue of $1.31 billion, up 29% from a year earlier and comfortably ahead of Wall Street estimates of $890.3 million, according to FactSet.

Moderna posted a profit of $162 million, reversing a loss of $200 million in the same period last year.

Earnings came in at 38 cents per share, compared with analyst expectations for a loss of $1.10 per share.

Shares surged 8.96% to $263.08 in trading.

The stock had already gained nearly 682% this year heading into Friday's session, reflecting growing investor interest in its experimental cancer vaccine and broader mRNA pipeline.

Covid vaccine sales drive Moderna's quarterly revenue

International demand for Moderna's Covid-19 vaccines played a significant role in the company's latest results.

The US market contributed $780 million in revenue, while international markets accounted for another $533 million.

Moderna attributed the increase to higher overseas vaccine sales and the execution of strategic partnerships with governments in the UK, Canada, and Australia.

The company also highlighted a five-year agreement with a local manufacturer in Mexico for COVID-19 vaccines, which it expects to support recurring revenue and expand its market presence.

Moderna's respiratory vaccine portfolio remains central to its business despite efforts to diversify into other areas.

In August, the US Food and Drug Administration approved its mRNA-based influenza vaccine, mFlusiva, for adults aged 50 and older.

The company is targeting a limited US launch during the upcoming flu season, as the approval came after the annual contracting cycle.

The vaccine also received regulatory clearance in Canada on Thursday, alongside a combination mRNA vaccine targeting both influenza and Covid-19.

Moderna raises full-year revenue growth forecast

Following its stronger-than-expected third-quarter performance, Moderna raised its full-year revenue growth forecast to between 15% and 25%, compared with its previous outlook of up to 10%.

The company expects revenue to be distributed roughly evenly between the US and international markets.

The improved outlook comes as Moderna works to stabilize its business following the decline in demand for Covid-19 vaccines after the pandemic.

Chief Executive Stephane Bancel said the company's financial recovery and manufacturing capabilities would help it expand into new areas of medicine.

"Moderna, unlike what most people thought a year ago, is not a Covid-19 company," Bancel said. "It's a broad mRNA platform company that happens to have its first product being a Covid-19 vaccine."

The company has approximately $8 billion in cash, which Bancel said would primarily support research and development.

"We think now is the time to invest," he added.

Cancer vaccine remains central to Moderna's growth strategy

While Covid-19 products continue to generate most of Moderna's revenue, investors are increasingly focused on its potential cancer treatments.

The company is developing intismeran autogene, a personalized melanoma vaccine, in partnership with Merck.

The treatment is being studied alongside Merck's Keytruda immunotherapy in patients at high risk of melanoma returning after surgery.

Expanded Phase 3 results showed that the combination reduced the risk of melanoma spreading or returning.

However, a data leak recently triggered an 18% single-session decline in Moderna shares.

Despite the setback, Moderna said it was working towards regulatory submissions and preparing for a potential commercial launch with Merck.

The partners are also exploring the treatment across other tumour types, as Moderna looks to expand its oncology pipeline.

data.title: US adds 165,000 jobs in October, crushing forecasts as Dec rate hike bets grow
data.description:
The US labour market delivered a stronger-than-expected performance in October, with employers adding significantly more jobs than economists had anticipated and the unemployment rate edging lower.

The figures could complicate the Federal Reserve's efforts to bring inflation under control and strengthen the case for another interest rate increase before the end of the year.

Nonfarm payrolls increased by a seasonally adjusted 165,000 in October, the Bureau of Labor Statistics reported on Friday.

The figure was substantially higher than the Dow Jones estimate of 59,000 and exceeded the average monthly gain of 48,000 recorded over the previous 12 months.

The unemployment rate declined to 4.1%, compared with economists' expectations of 4.2%.

The report also included significant upward revisions to employment figures for earlier months, suggesting that the labour market had been stronger than previously estimated.

August payroll growth was revised upwards by 53,000 to 186,000, while September's figure was increased by 31,000 to 60,000.

Wage growth raises fresh inflation concerns

The stronger employment figures were accompanied by an acceleration in wages.

Average hourly earnings increased 0.4% month-on-month and 3.1% year-on-year, compared with estimates of 0.3% and 2.9%, respectively.

The increase in wages could be particularly important for the Federal Reserve as it considers its next monetary policy decision.

Stronger pay growth can support household spending but may also add to inflationary pressures if businesses pass higher labour costs on to consumers.

Tom Graff, CIO at Facet, said the wage figures were more concerning for policymakers than the headline employment gains.

"This could be a one-month fluctuation, but it’s the fastest wage growth in nine months. Lack of immigration is creating a tighter labor market than the headline job gain figures would suggest. If this puts upward pressure on wages, it’s likely to feed inflation," Graff told Invezz.

Some economists have argued that the relatively low unemployment rate reflects a shrinking supply of available workers rather than exceptionally strong demand for labour.

Immigration restrictions and retirements could be contributing to that tighter supply.

Historically low layoffs and a recent increase in job openings have also raised concerns that competition for workers could intensify.

However, economists and US central bank officials have generally maintained that labour market conditions do not currently pose a significant inflation risk.

December rate hike bets increase

The employment report arrives at a sensitive point for the Federal Reserve.

The Fed left its benchmark overnight interest rate unchanged in a range of 3.75% to 4.00% last week.

However, stronger employment and wage growth have increased expectations that policymakers could resume tightening in December.

Traders raised the probability of a quarter-percentage-point increase at the Federal Open Market Committee's December 8-9 meeting to 76.8%, according to the CME Group's FedWatch tool.

The indicator pointed to only one additional increase after that meeting, while expectations for further hikes in 2027 have eased somewhat in recent days.

Graff said he did not expect the Fed to deliver an unusually large increase but believed policymakers could have to continue raising rates into next year.

"I don’t foresee the Fed doing anything as rash as hiking 50bps in December, but, in hindsight, they might wish they had fit two more hikes into 2026. As it is, I see the Fed hiking 25bps in December and probably at least two to three more times in the first half of 2027," Graff said.

Next Tuesday's consumer inflation report for October could provide further clues about the direction of monetary policy in early 2027.

Services sectors lead October hiring

The October employment gains were concentrated in professional and business services, healthcare, and transportation and warehousing.

Professional and business services added 70,000 jobs, significantly above the average monthly increase of 15,000 over the previous 12 months.

Professional, scientific and technical services accounted for 33,000 of those positions, while administrative and support services added 28,000.

Management of companies and enterprises contributed another 9,000.

The sector has added 269,000 jobs since reaching a recent low in October 2025.

Healthcare employment increased by 42,000, compared with an average monthly gain of 31,000 over the previous year.

Transportation and warehousing added 25,000 positions, including 17,000 jobs in couriers and messengers and 4,000 in air transportation.

The transportation and warehousing sector has added 104,000 jobs since a recent employment low in February, with couriers and messengers accounting for 71,000 of the increase.

Strong jobs data complicates outlook for technology stocks

The prospect of higher interest rates also presents a challenge for equity markets, particularly technology companies whose valuations are sensitive to borrowing costs and expectations of future earnings.

Nasdaq Composite rebounded on Friday as investors bought the dip in chip stocks following a sharp sell-off that had pushed the index into correction territory.

However, the stronger employment report sent Treasury yields higher, limiting gains in equity futures.

Nic Puckrin, a former Goldman Sachs analyst, said the figures were particularly unwelcome for technology stocks, which were already facing a severe downturn.

"It paves the way for rates to rise again in December and remain higher for longer – all bad news for tech valuations and the increasingly debt-fuelled AI buildout, especially now the sector is already being battered by expectations of stricter policies from the new Democratic Congress," he said.

He added that the report could give policymakers greater room to prioritise inflation control over employment concerns.

"The numbers give the Fed carte blanche to prioritise inflation over jobs, so ordinary Americans should prepare for a 0.25 percentage point rate hike in December. That means higher borrowing costs, more upward pressure on mortgage rates and less chance of a Santa rally for the stock market. However, it could also mean better returns on cash savings," he said.

The resilience of the labour market comes alongside strong economic growth.

US gross domestic product expanded at an annualised rate of 3.4% in the third quarter, supported by consumer spending and substantial business investment in artificial intelligence.

Graff warned that the scale of AI investment could itself contribute to inflationary pressures by increasing demand for resources and other inputs.

"The huge spending on AI is putting pressure on resources and prices. Higher rates are having some impact on AI investment, but it remains relatively minor. Maybe new restrictions on data centers will make a difference, but that is not at all assured. However, the Fed might have to hike enough to put real downward pressure on consumer spending to get inflation closer to target," Graff said.

The October report therefore presents the Fed with a difficult balance: a labour market that remains resilient, but wage growth and investment demand that could make its inflation objective harder to achieve.
